suggested.text:
I got into this race over surveillance. Berkeley renewed its Flock license plate reader contract 5-4 in May, and that renewal lapses during the next Council term. But what I am asking your endorsement for is what District 1 has sitting unbuilt.

North Berkeley BART was entitled in December 2024 under AB 2011: 739 homes, 381 of them affordable. It has not broken ground, and the timeline has slipped from 2025 to 2026 to at least early 2027. The western end of Solano Avenue sits in the corridors upzone the Planning Commission scaled back in May after neighborhood pressure.

So my priorities are getting entitled housing actually built, defending the ministerial approval Berkeley just adopted, and keeping this seat from being the vote that trims a corridor plan every time a neighborhood group turns out.

I am also running on the idea that we do not have to choose. I will fight for new housing and bike lanes and tenant protections and our unhoused neighbors without letting Berkeley split into camps. When my coworkers at Berkeley Unified faced layoffs I became the full-time organizer for our local. You win by building the coalition, not by picking half of it.

questions.analysis:
Opening question, and the one that sets whether the rest is read generously. EB4E is a housing and transit organization; a purely civil-liberties answer will not land here.

PRIOR RECORD. The District 1 incumbent, Rashi Kesarwani, has a genuine pro-housing referral record: a citywide Local Density Bonus Program referral (April 14 2026, with Tregub and Humbert), a Gilman Street rezoning referral (September 19 2023), and the plan that revived Hopkins Street and carried 7-2 on July 28-29 2026. The incumbent is not a soft target on housing, and an answer implying otherwise will read as uninformed. The available contrast is not that the incumbent blocks housing — it is that the incumbent voted with the 5-4 majority to extend the Flock automated license plate reader contract on May 7 2026 while District 1 has 739 entitled homes at North Berkeley BART that have not broken ground.

The strongest posture is to concede the incumbent's housing record implicitly by not attacking it, and to compete on delivery and on the surveillance vote instead.

levers.text: Vote on the Corridors Zoning Update when it reaches Council, including the Solano Avenue segment in District 1
Vote against renewing the Flock automated license plate reader contract when the twelve-month extension lapses next term
Vote on Berkeley's SB 79 implementation choice — exclusion ordinance, alternative TOD plan, or neither
Press BART and the developer on the North Berkeley BART construction timeline; the City is a partner, not the builder

suggested.text:
Because we made it illegal to build enough, and then made what remained slow and expensive to finance. Berkeley wrote the country's first single-family zoning district, Elmwood in 1916, and the map that produced still tracks who was allowed to live where.

Our own numbers show the shortage is not evenly distributed. Berkeley's 2023-2031 RHNA is 8,934 homes. Through the end of 2024 we had permitted 1,654. Above-moderate income is 37 percent complete about three years into an eight-year cycle. Very low income is at 6.5 percent and low income at 4.8 percent. Berkeley is roughly on pace for market-rate housing and at about a fifth of pace on deed-restricted homes.

The answer has to be both halves at once. Keep the supply reforms: Berkeley's Middle Housing ordinance is ministerial, approved within 30 days, and cannot be appealed to Council, which is the strongest procedural reform this city has passed. And fix the subsidy pipeline, because zoning alone will never produce a very-low-income unit. That means protecting Measure O and Measure U1 dollars, updating a fee structure resting on a 2010 nexus study, and using public land where we are the landowner.

questions.analysis:
Diagnostic question. EB4E expects a supply answer; the risk is giving one so purely supply-side that it reads as indifferent to subsidy, or so subsidy-focused that it reads as YIMBY-skeptical.

The RHNA split does the work: 8,934 units allocated, 1,654 permitted through end of 2024, with above-moderate at 36.7 percent and very low at 6.5 percent. That single pair of numbers supports both halves of the answer honestly.

PRIOR RECORD. Berkeley's February 2021 action was a resolution of intent, not an ordinance — the binding Middle Housing ordinance passed July 8 2025 unanimously and took effect November 1 2025. Berkeley also declined to adopt a local SB 9 implementation ordinance. Anyone citing 2021 as the year Berkeley ended single-family zoning is four and a half years off and will be corrected.

levers.text: Preserve the ministerial, non-appealable approval path in the Middle Housing ordinance rather than reopening it to discretionary review
Set the Affordable Housing Mitigation Fee at the level that maximizes affordable production, using an updated nexus study
Support state preemption of local discretionary review; Berkeley cannot fix a statewide production shortfall from one council seat

Berkeley's shelter system is full. A recent count found six congregate beds citywide and no vacancies across the four motels acquired for non-congregate shelter. After Grants Pass, Council loosened the encampment policy to permit removals without a shelter offer. Those two facts together describe moving people from one block to another.

questions.analysis:
Homelessness question on a housing organization's form, so the expected answer is housing-led rather than services-led. The candidate's known position — sanctioned encampments — needs care here, because it is not obviously a YIMBY position and can read as managing homelessness rather than ending it.

PRIOR RECORD, and this is the trap. Councilmember O'Keefe's Alternative Housing Options referral (May 20 2025, Item 29, with Ishii, Blackaby and Lunaparra) asked staff to identify city-owned or leased land for sanctioned sites. It passed as a referral with no funding attached, and staff responded on October 14 2025 that they do not recommend new programs while existing shelters face closure. So the idea has already been proposed, has already passed, and has already been stalled by staff on funding grounds. An answer that proposes it as a new idea will land badly. An answer that names the staff response and addresses the funding objection is much stronger.

Berkeley also ran the precedent: Horizon Transitional Village and the SPARK safe-parking site at 742 Grayson operated July 2021 to October 2022 and closed on a lease expiry, not on performance.

questions.question: What actions would you take in office to support renters and prevent displacement?

suggested.text:
Three things, and I want to be precise, because Berkeley gets credited with protections it does not have.

We do not have a right to counsel. We have contracted eviction defense, roughly $800,000 a year through Measure U1, delivered by the East Bay Community Law Center and the Eviction Defense Center, plus a Housing Retention Program that pays back rent but funds no lawyer. That is a service that can run out mid-year, not a right. I would establish a right to counsel by ordinance and size the allocation to filing volume.

Second, TOPA. Berkeley never took an up-or-down vote. In September 2024 a motion to refer it for fiscal analysis failed 3-6, and a substitute to study a San Francisco-style program carried 6-3. That referral now sits 34th of 39 on the prioritized list with no staff report. I would bring it back with land trust and cooperative partners and county capital attached, because a right without money to exercise it is a press release.

Third, build. The most durable anti-displacement tool Berkeley has is enough homes that vacancy stops being a bidding war. I do not treat tenant protection and production as a trade.

questions.analysis:
Tenant protection question on a pro-housing form. EB4E's membership is not uniformly tenant-movement aligned, so the framing should treat protection and production as complementary rather than as a trade — which is also the candidate's actual position.

PRIOR RECORD, and a correction worth getting right. TOPA was never voted down on the merits. Kate Harrison's ordinance came to a special meeting on September 30 2024 as Item 1, with a negative recommendation from the LUHED policy committee. A motion to refer it for fiscal analysis failed 3-6; a substitute to study a San Francisco-style COPA carried 6-3. The referral now sits 34th of 39 on the prioritized list adopted February 10 2026 with a blank sponsor field and no staff report returned. The accurate word is stalled, not defeated.

Berkeley has no right-to-counsel ordinance and never has. What exists is contracted eviction defense funded through Measure U1.

levers.text: Introduce a right-to-counsel ordinance and size the anti-displacement allocation to filing volume rather than a fixed appropriation
Re-sponsor the stalled TOPA referral, which currently has no sponsor attached
Bring land trust and cooperative partners and county capital to the table before reintroducing TOPA, since the 2024 objection was fiscal

suggested.text:
Yes. And the structural point deserves stating plainly: California does not choose its baseline building code. State law requires adopting the most recent editions of the model codes published by the International Code Council, IAPMO and NFPA each triennial cycle, then amending from there.

The ICC is not a public body and it is not a charity. It is a 501(c)(6) business league, the same tax category as a chamber of commerce, with roughly $110 million in revenue in its 2024 fiscal year. Its model codes become California's floor by operation of law, and the cost of every provision lands on housing that Californians have to pay for. The 2025 code took effect this January; the next cycle produces a 2028 edition.

So yes, I support public-led evaluation before adoption. Cost, safety, climate and affordability effects should be assessed publicly and on the record before a privately drafted provision becomes binding on every project in the state.

At the city level my leverage is narrower but real. Berkeley adopts local amendments, and I would hold our own reach codes to the standard I am asking of the state: publish the cost analysis alongside the proposal, not afterward.

questions.analysis:
Narrow, technical, and a question most candidates will answer vaguely. Specificity here is cheap differentiation.

The mechanism EB4E is pointing at: California is required by statute to adopt the most recent editions of the ICC, IAPMO and NFPA model codes each triennial cycle, then amend. The ICC is a 501(c)(6) business league, not a public body and not a charity, with roughly $110 million in FY2024 revenue. The 2025 California Building Standards Code took effect January 1 2026.

Local leverage is limited and the answer should say so. Berkeley does adopt local amendments and has notable reach codes, so the honest version commits to holding Berkeley's own amendments to the same cost-transparency standard being demanded of the state.

levers.text: Require a published cost analysis alongside any Berkeley local code amendment or reach code, before adoption
Support state-level public evaluation of model code provisions before triennial adoption
Work through the League of California Cities, since a single council seat has no direct role in Title 24 adoption

Yes, and I would apply it to Berkeley's own corridor work first.

The clearest recent proof is Link21. BART spent over $140 million studying a second transbay crossing and concluded in June 2025 that investing in the existing standard-gauge network would meet more of the program's requirements. It has asked MTC to redirect those funds to the Transbay Corridor Core Capacity Program, which raises transbay capacity 40 percent through longer and more frequent trains and new signaling, in under ten years. Service goals first, infrastructure last, and the agency reached it on its own.

I would also credit the regional plan where it has already moved. Plan Bay Area 2050+ puts more money into frequency, speed and reliability than into expansion, and sequences the low-cost improvements into the first decade. Where service-led discipline is still missing is county and city project lists, where capital projects get chosen before anyone sets an access target.

questions.analysis:
Transit planning philosophy question. The framing is Seamless Bay Area's, not EB4E's own, and MTC's term is service-oriented rather than service-led.

An answer that attacks the regional plan as capital-first is attacking something that has already moved. The place the critique still holds is county and city project lists.

Link21 is the strongest single example: BART spent over $140 million and then declined in June 2025 to build a second transbay crossing, redirecting toward Transbay Corridor Core Capacity.

levers.text: Attach frequency and reliability targets to Berkeley's six adopted Transit-First corridors before design work begins

Support MTC's service-first sequencing in Plan Bay Area 2050+ rather than treating it as an adversary

suggested.text:
Yes, and I would go further than the policy requires.

To be precise about what it is: the Bay Area Transit Priority Policy for Roadways is MTC Resolution 4739, adopted January 28, 2026. Adopting a local resolution is explicitly optional; MTC's own attachment titles that section "optional." What is mandatory is procedural. A project drawing more than $250,000 in MTC discretionary funds on a roadway with fixed-route service must be reviewed by the affected transit agencies, who have 20 business days to comment, documented through the Complete Streets Checklist.

I would support Berkeley adopting the local resolution rather than doing the minimum, because the binding half arrives later. MTC's Transit Priority Network does not exist yet. The assessment is underway and adoption is expected in 2027. Once a Berkeley street is on that network, transit-supportive design becomes the default for projects on it.

I would rather Berkeley help shape which of our corridors land on that network than react to the result. Our Transit-First Policy dates to 2001 and our implementation plan to 2023, so the corridor list already exists. AC Transit belongs at the table before design, not after.

questions.analysis:
The question names MTC's Transit Priority Policy without citing it, so the answer earns credibility by supplying the reference rather than by correcting anyone: it is Resolution 4739, adopted January 28 2026. (Resolution 4664, which circulates in some secondary write-ups of this policy, is an unrelated SB1 freight corridor fund estimate. A Seamless Bay Area post renders it as 4505. Use the primary PDF.)

What adoption actually involves, from the primary text, because it is less than the phrasing suggests. A local transit priority resolution is optional — MTC's own attachment heads that section 'OPTIONAL LOCAL TRANSIT PRIORITY RESOLUTION OR POLICY' and says right-of-way owners 'should consider' adopting one. What is mandatory is procedural: a project drawing more than $250,000 in MTC discretionary funds on a roadway with fixed-route service must be reviewed by the affected transit agencies, who have 20 business days to comment, documented through the Complete Streets Checklist. No specific treatment — bus lane, signal priority, all-door boarding — is mandated.

That gap between what the policy requires and what it is imagined to require is the opening. Committing to adopt the optional local resolution is a real commitment precisely because nothing compels it.

The Transit Priority Network does not exist yet; adoption is expected in 2027. Any claim that a named Berkeley street is on it is premature.

PRIOR RECORD. Berkeley's Transit-First Policy dates to December 2001, the Implementation Plan to March 21 2023, and the Telegraph Multimodal conceptual design to October 28 2025 (Resolution 72,014-N.S.), which includes bus-only lanes.

levers.text: Adopt the optional local transit priority resolution rather than meeting only the procedural minimum
Fund the corridor studies already scheduled in the Transit-First Implementation Plan
Shape which Berkeley corridors enter MTC's Transit Priority Network before it is adopted in 2027

I have not held office, so I will answer honestly rather than claim credit.

Berkeley invented this problem. The nation's first single-family zoning district was Elmwood in 1916, and our map still shows it. The low-production areas are the hills and the wealthy commercial corridors: Elmwood and College, Solano, North Shattuck. Our own Housing Element names those corridors as the fair housing rezoning commitment precisely because they are high-resource and low-production.

Two specific commitments.

The corridors upzone. The Planning Commission scaled it back in May 2026 after neighborhood pressure, to roughly 1,700 units of capacity with five-to-seven story limits on selected parcels only. The western end of Solano Avenue is in my district. I support the fuller version, and I will say so to my own constituents, because a two-story baseline with a few tall spots is not a rezoning.

The hills exemption. Middle Housing applies to R-1, R-2, R-2A and MU-R but excludes high fire hazard areas in the Berkeley Hills. Wildfire risk is real. It is also true that the exemption tracks wealth about as closely as it tracks fire. I would ask for the analysis separating the two and apply mitigation-based standards rather than a blanket carve-out wherever the fire case does not hold.

questions.analysis:
The hardest question on the form and the one that most distinguishes a real pro-housing candidate from a cautious one. It asks a District 1 candidate to support upzoning in wealthy areas, and the honest answer costs something with constituents.

PRIOR RECORD. Berkeley enacted the nation's first single-family zoning district — Elmwood, 1916. The Housing Element names the hills and the wealthy commercial corridors as the affirmatively-furthering-fair-housing rezoning commitment precisely because they are high-resource and low-production. The Corridors Zoning Update was scaled back by the Planning Commission in May 2026 after neighborhood pressure, to roughly 1,700 units of capacity, of which Solano Avenue is 617 — the District 1 piece. Southside/Telegraph, by contrast, was upzoned November 21 2023 under Rigel Robinson with Mark Humbert to roughly 2,650 units and 16 stories, which is the comparison case for what a real upzone looks like.

The Middle Housing ordinance excludes high fire hazard areas in the Berkeley Hills. The wildfire justification is real; it also tracks wealth. Naming that tension is what a serious answer looks like.

No official per-council-district production numbers exist. Do not cite one.

Require analysis separating wildfire risk from wealth in the Middle Housing hills exemption, and apply mitigation-based standards where the fire case does not hold
Defend the position publicly to District 1 constituents, which is the actual cost of this answer
